text:
The landlord tapes the notice where my mail used to land
Red ink on the first like a slap from a stranger's hand
I count the crumpled twenties in a coffee can of Folgers
Every bill a soldier, and I'm short by four soldiers
Space heater humming like it's begging for forgiveness
Fridge light the brightest thing that's working in this business
I sold the PlayStation, kept the cables in a tangle
Like I'm gonna buy it back if I just find the angle
Neighbor's TV leaking laugh tracks through the plaster
Every chuckle timed like it was written for disaster
I ran the numbers on a napkin from the Wendy's
Subtract the bus fare, still the math ain't friendly
The first of the month comes quicker than the fifteenth
Calendar's a loan shark, every square a missed rent
So I'm knocking on the office with a speech I rehearsed
Hoping that the man behind the glass was ever broke first

Clock in at eleven when the city's lungs collapse
Fluorescent hum the only hymn above the loading racks
I stock the cereal by aisle while the world's asleep
Tony the Tiger grinning like he knows my labor's cheap
Breakroom microwave rotating someone's lasagna
Forklift beeping backwards like a metronome for drama
My body's on a clock that never learned to read the sun
I eat my dinner at the hour other people's day is done
Supervisor's clipboard got my name squeezed in the margins
I'm the ghost inside the freezer, I'm the hand behind the bargains
Three a.m. the parking lot's a sea of sodium light
Moths conducting orchestras around the pole all night
I drive home while the joggers pass me stretching out their calves
Squinting at the sunrise like it only shines in halves
Blackout curtains duct-taped, and I sleep straight through the noon
My kids know my voice best through the wall of the next room

We shared a bunk bed, I was bottom, he was top
Every time he tossed I heard the springs above me pop
He taught me how to ride a bike by letting go too early
Gravel freckles on my knees and Mama's footsteps hurried
Now he calls collect, a robot voice says press five
Then his laugh comes through the static like it's barely still alive
I put money on his books like I'm feeding a meter
Every dollar is a promise that I'm still his keeper
He asks about the Raiders, asks if Pops is still drinking
I lie about the both of them to keep his head from sinking
The visiting room got vending machines and plastic chairs
We split a honey bun like we was kids again upstairs
He got my birthday on his wrist in shaky prison ink
A guitar string and a staple, more devotion than you'd think
When the guard calls time, he never hugs me long
Says go be the one of us the neighborhood got wrong

Linoleum peeling at the corners like old stamps
Mom stirring pinto beans beneath a sixty-watt lamp
Steam on the window where I finger-drew my name
Radio on oldies, every song about the same pain
She measured nothing, salt was in her palm and in her wrist
Recipes she never wrote, they lived inside her fist
Junk drawer full of twist ties, birthday candles, rubber bands
Coupons clipped and sorted like a general's commands
Kitchen table was the courtroom and the bank and the church
Where report cards got judged and where the bills got searched
I read her moods by how she brought the knife down on the board
Hard meant the job was killing her, soft meant she'd heard from the Lord
Now the house got sold, new owners painted it gray
But I can still smell cumin when I drive by on Fridays
I bought the same pot and I burned the beans the first try
Called her and she laughed so hard I heard her wipe her eye

A Polaroid curled in a shoebox under Auntie's bed
Cousin Dre at seventeen, a Starter cap, a high fade on his head
Detective left his card in ninety-nine, the ink is faded blue
She called it twice a year until the number went to someone new
The block knows who did it, it's a whisper with a limp
Walks into the corner store and buys the same lime Sprite and a fifth
Every candle on the curb has melted to a waxy plaque
Teddy bears turned gray from twenty winters on their back
Auntie keeps his room the way it was, a Walkman on the shelf
Tape still in it, side B, like he paused it for himself
The file's in a basement box beside a hundred more
Each one somebody's son, each one a closed door
I took the bus downtown and asked to see the folder
Clerk said it's archived, like the grief got any older
Some cases don't go cold, they just get quiet in the throat
Auntie still sets out his plate and still keeps his winter coat

My life is in a folder, carbon copies, staples rusted
Every pay stub proof I showed up when nobody trusted
Pink slip, W-2, a parking ticket out of Fresno
Court date on a napkin, child support in red, so
If you want to know me, don't ask what I believe
Pull my credit history and read it like a sleeve
Notary stamps raised like braille across my birth certificate
Mama's maiden name spelled wrong, a clerk thought it was different
I learned the government don't know you till you're paper
A social on a card, a name inside a skyscraper
They audit what I earn but never what I lost
Never itemize the nights, never deduct the cost
So I'm saving every envelope, the stamps, the postal marks
My grandkids gonna trace me like detectives in the dark
Every signature I wrote is me insisting I was here
Ink don't fade as fast as people do, that much is clear

Time and a half, but my body's paying double
Steel-toes laced so tight my ankles hum with trouble
Foreman says the line don't stop, so I don't stop
Vending machine coffee tasting like pennies and a mop
I'm counting hours like a gambler counting chips
Every hour fifty-something got a tremor in my grip
Wife texts goodnight with a photo of the twins
Asleep in matching dinosaurs, I zoom in on their chins
The check'll be fatter but the man'll be thinner
I missed the parent-teacher and the anniversary dinner
I bought her earrings with the extra from July
She wore them once to church and then she asked me why
Why the money always shows up but I don't
Why I say next month I'll slow down and I won't
Punching out at sunrise, the parking lot is gold
I'm trading all my young for a pension when I'm old

He came with a toolbox and a Buick that leaked
Mama's laugh came back, I hadn't heard it in weeks
I hated how he whistled when he fixed the kitchen sink
Hated that he always asked me what I really think
He never tried to be my father, never took the chair
Just left a plate of eggs out when nobody else was there
Taught me how to check the oil, how to change a tire
How to shake a hand like you ain't scared of a liar
I called him by his first name till I turned nineteen
Graduation, he was crying in the back row, unseen
My real dad sent a card that spelled my name with one less L
Steve drove four hours to my game and sat out in the hail
Now he's got a cane and a tremor in his hand
I mow his lawn on Sundays and I finally understand
Blood is just the ink, but love is who keeps writing
He signed for a son that wasn't his and kept on signing

The forty-two at midnight smells like fries and wet umbrellas
Driver's got a rosary that swings like a propeller
A nurse asleep in scrubs with her badge still clipped
A kid in a hoodie rapping softly, tapping on his hip
Reflection on the glass laid over shuttered shops
Like I'm a ghost haunting every one of my old stops
I count the stops by landmarks, not the names they print
The burned-out Taco Bell, the billboard selling mints
Somebody's arguing in Tagalog on the phone
Somebody's Bluetooth playing gospel, real low, alone
Miss this bus, it's an hour walking through the overpass
Where the sodium lights flicker and the gravel's full of glass
I pull the cord a stop early just to stretch my legs
Wind off the freeway tasting like the city's dregs
The driver nods goodnight like he's done it for a decade
Same nod every night, the only thanks I ever get paid

Got a plastic bracelet blinking green against my sock
Every step I take, a satellite is on the clock
Curfew's at nine, I watch the sunset through the screen door
Neighborhood's a movie I can't step into no more
Charger by the bed, I sleep tethered to the wall
Two hours every night like a phone that takes a call
Girl wants me at her cousin's quinceañera Saturday
I gotta file a form to tell the county where I'll be that day
I wear the long pants in July so no one sees the strap
Sweating through my denim, every summer is a trap
The beep goes off at Target in the cereal aisle
Lady grabs her kid and steers him past me with a plastic smile
They call it freedom with conditions, I call it a leash with Wi-Fi
Every heartbeat logged like I'm a suspect in my own life
Ninety days left, I'm counting backwards on the fridge
Crossing every square like I'm burning down a bridge

Fourteen-twelve after taxes, I read it at the bus stop
Some man named FICA took a cut, I never met him, felt robbed
Bought my mama groceries without looking at the price
Name-brand cereal, real butter, rib eye and the jasmine rice
Paid my phone bill in person just to watch them stamp it paid
Walked out like a senator who passed a law that day
Tried on some Jordans, put them back, the guilt was squeaking louder
Stashed the rest inside a sock behind a can of baby powder
Taped the stub inside my closet like a diploma on the wall
Sixteen and finally somebody owed me something, that's all
Manager said see you Monday like it was a promise
First time a grown man ever looked at me that honest
Dishwater on my wrists and the grease beneath my nails
I smelled like fryer oil, but my name came in the mail
Now I make way more and it never feels the same
Nothing hits like that first envelope that spelled my name

Vending machine hums a hymn in a key that's slightly flat
Pops behind a curtain, heart monitor tapping out its math
The floor's so waxed I see my worry walking under me
Nurses moving fast in sneakers soft as apologies
Chaplain with a clipboard asking if we need a prayer
I said I need a doctor, but I let him leave one there
Clock above the station's got a second hand that sticks
Every stutter makes me think about the thing it can't fix
Little sister sleeping on two chairs pushed together
Curled inside my hoodie like she's bracing for the weather
Cafeteria Jell-O the color of a stoplight
Uncle on the phone telling Georgia it's alright
It ain't alright, it's fluorescent and it's beige
Every room a sentence and the doors are turning pages
Doctor's walking slow, and I already know the walk
Some news don't need a word, the shoes do all the talk

Bulletproof glass and a bell that dings when I walk in
Owner's got a jeweler's loupe, a mustache and a grin
Guitars hung like hunting trophies on a pegboard wall
Wedding rings in rows, every one a little fall
I brought my grandpa's watch, a Bulova, gold plated
He weighs it on a scale like my memories get rated
Offers sixty dollars for the forty years it ran
I think about his wrist on the steering wheel of his van
A flat-screen with a crack, a trumpet with a dent
A stroller with the tags still on, somebody's month of rent
Every item got a ghost, a story on a string
A pawn ticket's just a promise folded up into a thing
I take the sixty and the ticket, ninety days plus interest plus pride
Fold it in my wallet by the prayer card where the important things hide
Day ninety-one I'm standing at the glass
Watching some stranger try it on, my grandpa's time just passed

Our family's a glass house with the curtains never drawn
Uncle preaching sober with a forty on the lawn
Auntie talks about my cousin's baby daddy at the cookout
While her husband's texting women that he thinks she won't find out
And me, I'm in the middle with my own cracks in the pane
Writing all their business down and calling it my pain
Every Thanksgiving is a trial without a judge
Mashed potatoes passed around with twenty years of grudge
Grandma says the grace and every head is bowed to hide
The way we size each other up like we're the ones who never lied
Windows fog from all the breathing, all the things we never say
Pie gets cut in silence, then the cousins drive away
I wanted to throw rocks, I had a pocket full of proof
Then I caught my own reflection, and my reflection had the truth
So I set the stones down, built a garden, row by row
In a glass house all you grow is what you're brave enough to show

Five-twenty on the score, it's a number that I wear
Like a scarlet tattoo that the banks can read from there
Car lot man was smiling till he ran my social
Then his face went flat like a tire in a pothole
Buy here, pay here, twenty-nine percent
On a Malibu with a hundred eighty thousand miles spent
I was nineteen with a Discover card and a dream
Bought a girl some Louis, now I'm paying for the seam
Collection agencies call me like an ex that won't move on
Same robot voice from Ohio every morning at dawn
Rent-to-own couch, I've paid it off three times
Still don't own a cushion, that's the crime without a crime
I tried a secured card with a two-hundred limit
Like the bank is holding training wheels and laughing at me in it
Seven years to fall off, that's the sentence that they gave
I'm laying on-time payments like the bricks to climb out of the grave

Mama ironing my shirt while the gospel station plays
Starch so stiff the collar's got opinions on my ways
Pews of sticky varnish and the fans got funeral ads
Deacon Wallace nodding off and snoring like he's glad
Pastor sweating through his robe about the tithe and Pharaoh
Church ladies in their hats like satellites in a row
Organ player's riff got more soul than the radio
Choir hits the high note and the windows almost go
I'm thirteen and bored, drawing rappers on the program
But when Grandma starts to cry, I don't know what to do with my hands
She's praising for a son that's in a cell in Lompoc
Thanking God for things I'd call a curse, but she don't stop
Afterward the fellowship hall with the chicken and sweet tea
Everybody hugging like they ain't been texting gossip all week
I ain't been in years, but on Sundays around noon
I iron my own shirt and I hum her favorite tune

The door chime's like a doorbell at a second home
Mr. Park behind the plexi with his radio and his comb
Hot Cheetos and an Arizona, ninety-nine cents for years
Inflation hit the whole world but that can stayed in the clear
Lotto tickets scratched with dimes by men who swear today's the day
Silver shavings on the counter like the hopes they blew away
He let me run a tab when Mama's check was late again
Wrote it in a notebook, never interest, never asked me when
Cats asleep on the bread rack, a mop bucket by the beer
Security camera that's been blinking red for a year
Every fight out front, he watched it through the plexiglass
Then came out with a broom and swept away the broken glass
Now they're turning it to juice behind a reclaimed wooden sign
Twelve-dollar smoothies where my tab used to be signed
Mr. Park retired to his daughter's place in Queens
I still owe him four dollars and I know just what it means

I still know Tasha's landline, seven digits and a cord
Her mama picked up every time like a bouncer at the door
Granddad's number's in my thumbs, I dial it when I'm stressed
It rings a stranger in Modesto who gets real obsessed
With asking who this is, and I can't explain the ache
So I hang up and sit inside the silence that I make
My contacts full of ghosts with names like Big Mike Cell
Mike's been gone since twenty-twelve, I keep him like a shell
Disconnected tones play like a three-note lullaby
The number you have reached has learned to say goodbye
Old flip phone in a drawer, it won't even hold a charge
But the voicemails inside it make the little thing feel large
Mama's voice from oh-nine saying baby, call me back
I never did that night, and now I'm calling through the cracks
Every number's a key to a house that's not around
I memorize the locks long after they tore it down

She's turning seven and she wants a unicorn with wings
I'm on YouTube at two a.m. learning how to pipe the icing rings
Bought a cake from Costco, scraped the logo off with care
Wrote her name in purple and it slumped like it was scared
Balloons from Dollar Tree, I blew till my head was spinning
Twenty little paper plates with princesses all grinning
Her mama and me ain't talked since the custody hearing
But we both lean in when she blows, and for a second we're both cheering
She closed her eyes so tight to make the wish, her nose scrunched up
I wished that every other weekend someday could be enough
Gift bag full of tissue paper hiding something small
A locket with a photo from the hospital, that's all
She opened it and asked me who's the baby, who's the guy
I said that's us the first day, she said Daddy, why you cry
I said it's frosting in my eye, she wiped it with her sleeve
Seven candles smoking and I'm the one who don't want to leave

Black trash bag of clothes, that's the luggage of the system
Five houses by eleven, I could draw you every kitchen in them
Every house got rules taped to the fridge in different fonts
Don't eat after nine, ask before you take the bread you want
Social worker with a lanyard and a Honda full of files
Calls me buddy on the drive like she's counting off the miles
I learned to read a mood in how a bedroom door closes
How a woman says goodnight, if it's love or just the motions
Never unpacked, I kept my sneakers by the bed
Like any night a knock could come and move me somewhere else instead
Birthdays were a cupcake from a stranger's good intention
Report cards signed by names I couldn't spell in the section
Aged out at eighteen with a check and a bus pass
And a folder of my life you could flip through pretty fast
Now I got a key that's mine, I sleep with the door unlocked
Just to know that no one's coming, just to feel the clock stop

Alarm at four-fifteen, the phone screen like a slap
Snooze button worn smooth from my thumb's tired tap
Coffee in a thermos that my father used to carry
Dented on the side from when he dropped it at the ferry
Black jeans, same hoodie, with the smell of yesterday's bleach
Waiting on the bus with the moon still out of reach
Same faces every morning, never learned a single name
The lady with the crossword, the old man with the cane
We're a congregation praying for the clock to move
Punching in like penitents with nothing left to prove
Again, again, again, the word's a hammer on a nail
My life's a loop of Mondays and my Friday's in the mail
I'm twenty-eight, my knees already crackle like a fire
Manager don't know I write these bars on boxes by the dryer
Every shift I clock in, I leave a line behind
Someday these early mornings gonna pay me back in kind

Chain-link fence with a hole the shape of every kid
Sneaking in to play two-hand touch, that's what we did
Broken glass like diamonds in the weeds and in the dirt
A shopping cart tipped over like it's sleeping off the hurt
Used to be a laundromat before the fire in oh-six
Now it's dandelions, mattresses, and busted bricks
City put a sign up, Coming Soon, Mixed Use
That sign's been coming soon since I was learning to tie shoes
We built a fort from pallets and we called it our republic
Our flag a Raiders T-shirt on a broom, and nobody could touch it
Ray had his first kiss behind the rusted Ford
Junior lost his first fight there and swore he'd even the score
Now there's surveyors in vests with their tripods and their stakes
Pink tape on the sticks marking up what someone takes
Condos going up where our republic used to sprawl
Nobody's gonna know we ever ruled there at all

Engine running in the Walgreens lot at one a.m.
Forehead on the steering wheel, too tired to pretend
I ain't been to church since Grandma's homegoing in May
But the dashboard is an altar, so I bow my head and pray
Lord, it's me, the one who only calls when things are cracked
The check engine light is glowing like at least it's got my back
Sodium lamp buzzing like it's speaking in tongues
A cart rolls by itself like it's got somewhere to run
I prayed for my brother's lawyer, for my baby's ear infection
For the transmission in this Camry and a little bit of direction
A security guard knocks and asks me if I'm good
I said I'm talking to somebody, and he nodded like he understood
He said he does the same on breaks out by the dumpster
Whole city full of people praying where nobody would suspect them
Amen comes out foggy on the window, then it fades
I wipe it with my sleeve, put it in drive and count the days

Ten deep at the birthday when I had the section booked
Two deep at the courthouse, and one of them was crooked
Marcus borrowed eight hundred for his daughter's braces
Then I saw him on his story at a Raiders game in Vegas
Group chat went quiet the week my lights went out
Read receipts lit up like a stadium, but nobody spoke out
Real problems don't care about your follower count
The landlord don't accept retweets as a payment amount
I learned who's a friend by who shows up with a dolly
On moving day at seven, not at nine for the party
Junebug did, he ain't got much, but he brought a truck
And a cooler full of baloney and a pocket full of luck
The fake ones send a heart emoji when your granny passes
The real ones stay and stack the chairs and sweep up after masses
I ain't bitter, I just did the math and trimmed the list to three
Fewer names inside my phone, but every one would bleed for me

Mornings at the warehouse scanning boxes till the beep
Evenings at the Panda Express in the orange-chicken heat
Two uniforms in my backseat, I change at red lights
Khaki for the sunlight, black apron for the night
Microwaved burrito on my lap, my lunch break's like a pit stop
Twenty-minute nap with the seat back and the windows cracked up top
Two W-2s and still a single-parent budget
Two managers who both think I'm theirs, and both of them can judge it
My son's asleep when I leave and asleep when I come back
I know him by the cereal bowls he leaves out in a stack
His teacher emails me at times when I'm frying rice
I read it on the sneeze guard, wipe the screen and read it twice
Thirty-two years old and my body's double-booked
Back aches like it's working a third job I never took
They say work smarter, man, I'm working both the clocks
Two jobs and still one key that barely turns the locks

Plastic on the sofa squeaking every time you sat
Doilies under lamps, a velvet Jesus by the welcome mat
Candy dish of butterscotch that nobody ever ate
Melted in a lump, a sugar paperweight
Wall of school pictures, every cousin's gap-toothed grin
Laser backgrounds, crooked collars, she framed every one of them
Kitchen always smelling like the collard greens and Pine-Sol
Her slippers whispering a sermon down the hall
She kept a coffee can of bacon grease beside the stove
And twenty dollars in her Bible in the Book of Job
That house was where we landed when the world threw us out
Every cousin did a season on that squeaky pullout
Some flipper's gonna gut it and paint the paneling gray
Rip the plastic off the sofa that she saved for Judgment Day
I kept the candy dish, that stubborn lump of gold
And the twenty in the Bible, 'cause some things you don't fold

Bought it at the Men's Wearhouse for Junior in oh-nine
Charcoal, two buttons, pants hemmed a little high
Since then it's been to Pooh's, then Lil Ant's, then Uncle Rome
That suit's seen more of cemeteries than it's ever seen of home
Dry cleaner knows the jacket, says again, and I just nod
Plastic over shoulders like a body bag for cloth
Inside pocket's stacked with programs, all the obituaries creased
Faces smiling up from cardstock, rest in power, rest in peace
Never wore it to a wedding, never wore it to a dance
Never to a job interview, a prom, a second chance
It's tight around the shoulders now, I grew, the dead did not
They stay the age they left at, frozen in the plot
I keep it in the closet, way back behind the coats
Like if I hide it deep enough the phone won't clear its throat
Mama says to get another one, a black one, better fit
I said this one knows the way, I'm just the one inside of it

Popcorn ceiling got a water stain shaped like Ohio
I've mapped every county while my thoughts play in full stereo
Fan blade wobbling on a loose screw, tick, tick, tick
Every wobble is a question that I never answer quick
Phone face-down on the nightstand glowing through the wood
Notifications from a group chat that ain't doing me no good
Replay the meeting where I froze up when my boss said my name
Rewrite it with a comeback, but the ending stays the same
The fridge kicks on downstairs like it's shrugging off a cough
A car alarm two blocks away that no one's turning off
Three a.m.'s a courtroom where I'm the judge and the defendant
Every bill is evidence and every text a witness pending
I think about my pops at my age, did he stare like this
At a ceiling out in Fresno, adding up what he would miss
The digital clock goes three-oh-eight, then three-oh-nine
The ceiling never answers, but it listens every time

U-Haul ten-footer with a dent across the ramp
Mama on the porch in her robe, her coffee going damp
Taped the boxes, wrote kitchen, books and misc in Sharpie
Found my old Pokémon cards and a picture from a party
My room is just a carpet with four dents and a lighter square
Where the poster blocked the sun nine years, the paint is fresher there
Little brother claims my room like he ain't sad about it
Turning up his game so loud that I can hear him doubt it
Pops helped me carry the dresser, didn't say a word
Just grunted on the stairs, but it was the loudest thing I heard
Studio apartment forty minutes up the Five
First night the silence hummed like something barely alive
No one yelling dinner, no one hogging the shower
I ate cereal for dinner like a king, then cried for an hour
Called home just to hear the TV in the background
Mama said your plate's still here, and that's the realest sound

Nothing was a mattress on the floor without a frame
Mail addressed to tenants who'd been gone before we came
Nothing was the light bill in an envelope that's pink
Washing socks with dish soap in a rusted kitchen sink
Nothing had a smell, the mildew in the hallway carpet
Nothing had a taste, the generic flakes from the market
So when they ask me where I came from, don't expect a myth
I won't say I rose from ashes, I just rose from what was left
I'm talking nine-to-fives and night school at the college
Library late fees on the books that gave me knowledge
Something is a lease where my name is spelled correct
A fridge that hums with groceries, a direct deposit check
Something is my mama sleeping in past seven on a weekday
No alarm, no double shift, no bus to catch, no cheap pay
Something ain't a mansion, it's a mattress with a frame
And a mailbox where the only letters carry our real name
